meta.title: Agent Production Readiness Scorecard
meta.description: Twelve questions that separate an AI agent demo from a system you can bill customers for. Scored across reliability, cost control, and observability.

pillars.name: Reliability
pillars.blurb: Can you prove it still works after a change?

pillars.name: Cost & latency
pillars.blurb: Do you know what a conversation costs and how slow it gets?

pillars.name: Observability
pillars.blurb: When it fails at 2am, can you find out why?

questions.question: Do you have an automated eval suite that runs when a prompt or model changes?
questions.help: Not unit tests on your glue code — evals on the agent's actual outputs against known-good cases.

options.label: No — we try a few prompts by hand
A handful of ad-hoc cases in a notebook
A real suite, but someone runs it manually
In CI, with a pass threshold that blocks merges

gap.title: No regression safety net on agent behaviour
gap.consequence: Every prompt tweak is an unmeasured bet. You will ship a regression, hear about it from a customer, and have no way to tell which change caused it.
gap.fix: Freeze 30–50 real inputs with expected outcomes, score them with a mix of assertions and LLM-as-judge, and gate merges on the aggregate.
gap.effort: 3–5 days for a first suite that pays for itself immediately
gap.businessRisk: You cannot tell whether a change made the product better or worse. Every quality decision is currently a guess.

questions.question: Are your eval cases drawn from real production traffic?
questions.help: Synthetic examples written by the team systematically miss the inputs that actually break agents.

options.label: We have no eval cases
All hand-written by the team
Some real traffic, added occasionally
Failures from production flow back into the suite routinely

gap.title: Evals do not reflect real user behaviour
gap.consequence: Your suite passes while real users hit failures nobody imagined. Confidence goes up, quality does not.
gap.fix: Add a one-click 'capture this run as an eval case' path from your trace viewer, and make triaging new failures a weekly ritual.
gap.businessRisk: Testing reflects what the team imagined users would do, not what they actually do.

questions.question: Are prompts versioned and tied to the deployment that used them?
questions.help: If a customer reports a bad answer from last Tuesday, can you reconstruct the exact prompt that produced it?

options.label: Prompts are edited in a dashboard or hardcoded inline
In git, but no link from a response back to a version
Versioned and logged per request
Versioned, logged, and independently rollback-able

gap.title: Prompt changes are untraceable
gap.consequence: Debugging becomes archaeology. You cannot reproduce a reported failure, so you cannot confirm a fix.
gap.fix: Treat prompts as versioned artefacts in git, stamp the version onto every trace, and make rollback a deploy-free operation.
gap.businessRisk: A complaint from last month cannot be investigated, reproduced, or confirmed fixed.

questions.question: Are tool-call arguments validated before execution?
questions.help: Models hallucinate arguments: wrong types, invented IDs, out-of-range values, occasionally destructive ones.

options.label: No — we pass model output straight through
Loose checks on some tools
Schema validation on every tool
Schema validation plus authorisation checks and dry-run on destructive tools

gap.title: Hallucinated tool arguments reach real systems
gap.consequence: This is the failure mode that causes actual damage rather than just a bad answer — wrong record updated, wrong customer emailed, wrong row deleted.
gap.fix: Validate every tool input against a strict schema, re-check authorisation server-side rather than trusting the agent, and require confirmation for irreversible actions.
gap.effort: 2–4 days, and the highest-value work on this list
gap.businessRisk: The agent can act on invented data — updating the wrong record or contacting the wrong customer.

questions.question: Do you know the token cost of a single average conversation?
questions.help: A number, not an estimate — attributable per feature, per tenant, or per customer.

options.label: No — we see one total on the provider invoice
We can estimate it roughly
Measured per conversation in aggregate
Attributed per feature and per tenant, on a dashboard

gap.title: Unit economics are invisible
gap.consequence: You cannot price your product, forecast spend, or tell which feature is quietly consuming the budget. Cost surprises arrive monthly.
gap.fix: Log token counts and computed cost on every call with feature and tenant tags, then chart cost per conversation as a first-class product metric.
gap.businessRisk: You cannot price the product, forecast spend, or say which feature is consuming the budget.

questions.question: Is there a hard ceiling that stops runaway spend?
questions.help: Per-request token caps, per-user daily limits, a global circuit breaker — something that fails closed.

options.label: No limits anywhere
Provider-level budget alerts only
Per-request caps in place
Per-request, per-user and global breakers, all tested

gap.title: No circuit breaker on spend
gap.consequence: One looping agent, one adversarial user, or one bad deploy can produce a five-figure bill over a weekend. Alerts notify you after the money is gone.
gap.fix: Enforce max token caps per request, rate limits per user per day, and a global kill switch that degrades to a cheaper model or a queue rather than spending without bound.
gap.businessRisk: One malfunction or one abusive user can produce a five-figure bill over a weekend.

questions.question: Do you route different tasks to different models by difficulty?
questions.help: Classification, extraction, and formatting rarely need your most expensive model.

options.label: One model handles everything
We picked cheaper models in a couple of places by hand
Deliberate routing per task type
Routing plus caching, with quality measured per tier

gap.title: Paying premium rates for trivial work
gap.consequence: Usually the single largest recoverable line item — often 40–70% of spend on sub-tasks a much cheaper model handles at equal quality.
gap.fix: Classify tasks by required capability, route accordingly, add prompt caching on stable system context, and verify quality per tier with your eval suite.
gap.effort: 3–5 days, typically the fastest measurable ROI
gap.businessRisk: You are paying premium rates for work a cheaper model does identically — usually the largest recoverable cost.

questions.question: Do you track p95 latency per agent operation, not just the average?
questions.help: Averages hide the multi-step runs where users give up and leave.

options.label: We do not measure latency
Averages only
p95 tracked overall
p95 and p99 per operation, with alert thresholds

gap.title: Tail latency is unmeasured
gap.consequence: The average looks acceptable while a meaningful slice of users waits 40 seconds and abandons. Retries and multi-step chains live entirely in that tail.
gap.fix: Instrument per-step timing, alert on p95 by operation, and set an explicit latency budget that streaming or partial results must satisfy.
gap.businessRisk: Some users wait long enough to give up, and it is invisible in the averages you currently see.

questions.question: Can you replay a single agent run end to end — every step, prompt, and tool call?
questions.help: One trace ID that shows the whole decision path, not scattered log lines.

options.label: Application logs only
We log prompts and responses, unlinked
Traces per run, retained briefly
Full step-level traces, searchable, retained long enough to investigate

gap.title: No per-run trace
gap.consequence: Every investigation starts from zero. Mean time to diagnosis is measured in days, and some failures are simply never explained.
gap.fix: Adopt step-level tracing (OpenTelemetry or a purpose-built LLM observability tool), propagate one trace ID across the whole run, and make traces searchable by user and outcome.
gap.businessRisk: When something goes wrong nobody can explain why. Investigations take days or never conclude.

questions.question: Does your team have shared, named categories for how the agent fails?
questions.help: "Tool argument hallucination" and "retrieval miss" are categories. "It was wrong" is not.

options.label: Failures are described case by case
Informal shared intuition, nothing written down
A documented taxonomy
A taxonomy that every failure is classified against, with trend tracking

gap.title: Failures cannot be counted, so they cannot be prioritised
gap.consequence: Without categories there are no rates. The team fixes whatever was complained about loudest rather than what happens most.
gap.fix: Name your failure modes, tag every incident against them, and review the distribution monthly. Fix by frequency times severity.
gap.effort: 1–2 days to define, ongoing to maintain
gap.businessRisk: Failures cannot be counted, so the team fixes what was complained about loudest rather than what happens most.

questions.question: Are outputs checked for policy, PII, and grounding before reaching the user?
questions.help: Especially relevant if the agent touches customer, financial, or health data.

options.label: No checks
Prompt instructions telling the model to behave
Programmatic checks on some paths
Enforced checks on every path, with blocked outputs logged

gap.title: Guardrails rely on the model following instructions
gap.consequence: Prompt-based rules are advisory, not enforcement. One jailbreak or one unusual input and unreviewed content — or someone else's data — reaches a user.
gap.fix: Enforce checks in code outside the model: PII detection, policy classifiers, and grounding verification against retrieved sources. Log every block as a signal.
gap.businessRisk: Unreviewed content, or another customer’s data, can reach a user.

questions.question: Is there a named person accountable for whether the agent works?
questions.help: Not the whole team, and not the person who happens to be on call.

options.label: Nobody in particular
Shared across the team informally
One owner, among many other duties
A named owner with time allocated and metrics they report on

gap.title: Agent quality is nobody's job
gap.consequence: Reliability work loses to feature work every sprint, because features have an owner arguing for them and reliability does not.
gap.fix: Name an owner, give them explicit time, and have them report a small number of reliability metrics on the same cadence as product metrics.
gap.effort: An organisational decision, not an engineering one
gap.businessRisk: Nobody is accountable for whether this works, so reliability loses to feature work every sprint.

bands.label: Prototype
bands.verdict: This is a demo with users attached. That is not a criticism — it is a very common and very risky place to be.
bands.recommendation: Do not add features yet. The four critical gaps below are the ones that cause incidents, and each is a few days of work.

bands.label: Fragile
bands.verdict: Some instincts are right, but the safety net has holes in exactly the places that produce 2am pages.
bands.recommendation: Close the critical gaps first, then build the eval suite that stops you regressing what you just fixed.

bands.label: Hardening
bands.verdict: You are meaningfully ahead of most teams shipping agents today. What is missing is consistency rather than awareness.
bands.recommendation: Make the practices you already have partial coverage on universal, and start tracking failure rates by category so you can prioritise by data.

bands.label: Production-grade
bands.verdict: This is a system you can defensibly bill customers for.
bands.recommendation: The remaining wins are efficiency rather than safety: model routing, caching, and tightening latency budgets.

bands.label: Exemplary
bands.verdict: Genuinely rare. You are running agents with more discipline than most teams apply to conventional services.
bands.recommendation: You probably do not need me. If you would like a second pair of eyes on the edges, I am happy to talk — but I would say so if I could not add value.

decisions.line: No action needed beyond efficiency work. Recheck in six months or after a significant change.
No emergency. Schedule the highest-risk gaps within the quarter — none of them are large.
Schedule the critical gaps into the next sprint. Everything else can wait.
Pause new agent features until the critical gaps are closed. This is days of engineering work, not quarters.
